questions.q: State the standard duration of an accounting period as per the Companies Act 2013 and Income Tax Act in India, and name the typical financial year period followed by Indian companies.
questions.a: The standard duration is 12 months (one year). The typical financial year in India runs from April 1 to March 31. A wrong answer (e.g., "calendar year January–December" or "6 months") reveals the student confuses the statutory financial year with the calendar year or interim reporting periods, indicating they have not internalised the legal framework governing accounting periods in India.

questions.q: A student argues: "Since the Going Concern Concept assumes the business will continue indefinitely, we don't need artificial accounting periods — we can just calculate profit when the business finally closes." Explain why this reasoning is flawed using the purpose of accounting information for external users.
questions.a: The reasoning is flawed because external users (investors, creditors, tax authorities) need timely, periodic information for decision-making — a bank assessing loan repayment capacity cannot wait for liquidation; tax authorities require annual tax computation; investors compare year-on-year performance. The Going Concern Concept justifies spreading asset costs over multiple periods (depreciation), but the Accounting Period Concept creates the periodic checkpoints for reporting. A wrong answer that conflates the two concepts shows the student cannot distinguish between the *assumption of continuity* (going concern) and the *need for periodic measurement* (accounting period).

questions.q: M/s Sharma Traders, a proprietorship firm, follows the financial year April 1 – March 31. On March 28, 2024, they sold goods worth ₹50,000 on credit to a customer. The customer paid on April 5, 2024. Under the Accounting Period Concept combined with the Accrual Basis, in which accounting period should this revenue be recognised? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Revenue should be recognised in the accounting period ending March 31, 2024 (FY 2023–24). The Accounting Period Concept requires drawing a line at March 31; the Accrual Basis (which this concept enables) recognises revenue when the legal right to receive it arises (sale completed/goods delivered), not when cash is received. Since the sale occurred on March 28, it belongs to FY 2023–24. A wrong answer placing it in April 2024 reveals the student is applying Cash Basis thinking and has not grasped that the Accounting Period Concept works with Accrual Basis to assign transactions to the correct period based on economic occurrence, not cash flow.

questions.q: Compare the accounting period requirements for: (a) a listed company on NSE, (b) a partnership firm retiring a partner on September 30, and (c) a sole proprietorship with no external reporting obligations. How does the Accounting Period Concept apply differently in each case?
questions.a: (a) Listed company: Must prepare annual financial statements (April–March) AND quarterly interim statements (every 3 months) per SEBI LODR Regulations — the Accounting Period Concept mandates shorter sub-periods for timely market disclosure. (b) Partnership firm: On partner retirement, an interim accounting period is created from the last balance sheet date to the retirement date (e.g., April 1 – Sept 30) to settle the retiring partner's capital — the concept adapts to a specific event-driven cutoff. (c) Sole proprietorship: Legally only requires annual statements for tax (Income Tax Act), but may choose monthly/quarterly for internal management — the concept's rigidity varies with user needs. A wrong answer treating all three identically shows the student sees the accounting period as a rigid rule rather than a flexible framework driven by user information needs and legal requirements.

questions.q: Critique the following statement: "The Accounting Period Concept is just an administrative convenience; it has no impact on the actual profitability or financial position of the business." Use the concepts of revenue recognition, expense matching, and comparability in your evaluation.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. The Accounting Period Concept directly shapes reported profitability through its interaction with Revenue Recognition (when to record sales) and Matching (which expenses offset which revenues). For example, a December 2023 sale with cash received in January 2024 shifts revenue between periods, altering profit figures for both years. It enables inter-period comparability (trend analysis) and inter-firm comparability (standardised reporting dates). Without it, profit measurement would be arbitrary and non-comparable. A wrong answer agreeing with the statement reveals the student views accounting periods as mere calendar compliance rather than understanding that period boundaries determine which revenues match which expenses — the very foundation of periodic profit calculation.

questions.q: Design a scenario where a business changes its accounting period from the standard April–March financial year to a calendar year (January–December) with regulatory approval. Identify three specific accounting challenges this change creates for revenue recognition, expense matching, and comparative financial statements, and propose how each should be handled per the Consistency and Full Disclosure concepts.
questions.a: Scenario: An Indian subsidiary of a US multinational changes its accounting period to January–December to align with the parent's reporting calendar, with ROC approval. Challenges: (1) Revenue recognition: A long-term construction contract spanning the transition period (e.g., Oct 2023 – Mar 2024) must have revenue allocated between the old 9-month period (Apr–Dec 2023) and new 12-month period (Jan–Dec 2024) using percentage-of-completion — handled by applying Revenue Recognition consistently to each sub-period. (2) Expense matching: Depreciation for FY 2023–24 (12 months) vs. the new 9-month period (Apr–Dec 2023) requires prorating — handled by matching depreciation expense to the shortened period's revenue. (3) Comparative statements: The first new annual report (Jan–Dec 2024) lacks a prior-year comparable (Jan–Dec 2023) — handled by Full Disclosure: presenting 15-month comparatives (Apr 2023–Dec 2024) or restating prior periods with clear notes. A poor answer that ignores the Consistency/Full Disclosure interplay shows the student cannot integrate multiple concepts to solve real-world period-change problems.
